## How to Plan a Wedding That Fits Your Budget


---


**Key Takeaways:**


- Decide **what matters most to both of you** , then determine where you're comfortable spending more and where you can save.
- Before borrowing to pay for your wedding, consider how the payments and interest could affect your finances after the celebration.
- Work backward from your wedding date to create a realistic monthly savings goal.


From the guest list and venue to favors and attire, wedding expenses can add up quickly.


According to a 2026[Zola survey](https://www.zola.com/expert-advice/the-first-look-report-2026) , couples expected to spend an average of $36,000 on their weddings, with 52% putting other financial milestones on hold.


Many see the high cost of a wedding as unavoidable, but other couples are considering what they actually want to spend money on. That could mean splurging on a live band while keeping the guest list small or choosing an inexpensive venue to make room for pricey photography.


Your wedding can reflect what matters to both of you. A realistic budget can help you understand the trade-offs and spend more intentionally.


## Begin with priorities, not the price tag


Before you start a Pinterest board or tour venues, identify your top three wedding priorities. What elements matter most to both of you?


It could be:


- Food and drinks
- Photography and video
- Music (DJ or live band)
- Venue
- Decor
- Honeymoon
- Guest list size


You can start with each person independently naming three things they care most about spending on. Compare lists and find the overlap.


Similarly, it's important to talk about what you don’t care about as much. For example, if neither of you cares about florals, that could be a category to spend less on. Creating those boundaries early on can help avoid unnecessary spending and people-pleasing that can come with wedding planning.


## Break the budget into “must-haves,” “nice-to-haves” and “not-for-us”


After your priorities are solidified, it’s time to talk numbers. Creating a budget out of thin air can feel intimidating, so consider starting with buckets.


Divide each potential expense into three categories:


- Must-haves, or things you’d regret skipping
- Nice-to-haves, or things you’d enjoy, but could cut if you have to
- Not-for-us, or things you don’t want to spend on


Sorting expenses into these categories can make it easier to say no to costs that don’t support your priorities.


As you sort through spending, don’t forget costs such as alterations, gratuities, vendor fees, a marriage license and more. And the buckets can exist beyond the planning stage. Each time a new cost crops up in the planning process, which it will, you can revisit the list and ask, “Is spending on XYZ actually worth moving money away from something else?”


Establish a total comfortable budget based on what you can afford, not just what weddings typically cost or what your friends may have spent on their weddings. Separate money you already have from money you expect to save before the wedding. Then, build in a buffer for unexpected costs, instead of earmarking every dollar to planned expenses.


## Find where you can cut, without feeling cheap


Rather than focusing on cutting the budget across the board, focus on cutting what guests are least likely to notice, or what you don’t personally value.


Category


If this is a priority


If you'd rather save


**Guest List** Large guest list A smaller guest list can cut food, drink, rental and venue costs


**Date/Time** Evening, weekend wedding during high season An off-season, weekday or brunch wedding


**Decor** Design elements on every surface A few, high-impact design elements


**Invitations** High-end stationery for save-the-dates and wedding invitations Digital invitations


**Favors** Genuinely useful or well-made thank-you gifts Skipping favors if they feel unnecessary


**Flowers** Large arrangements on every table Seasonal blooms or fewer arrangements


**Attire** Custom wedding attire Secondhand or rented day-of outfits


**Wedding party** A large wedding party
of family and friends A smaller wedding party can save on expenses like bouquets, boutonnieres, gifts and more


Remember, you don’t need to cut costs everywhere, but strategically cut back on expenses that won’t meaningfully change your wedding day experience. This can free up more of your budget for splurge categories.


## Don't let the wedding budget become your entire financial plan


Your wedding may be a big, important event, but it’s likely just one of your many financial goals as a couple.


Before you start aggressively saving (or spending) for the wedding, make sure you're still making progress toward other priorities. Consider how wedding savings will fit alongside your other financial priorities.


As a couple, review your progress toward:


- Emergency savings
- [Retirement contributions](https://financialwellnesscenter.northwest.bank/retirement-planning/saving/article/getting-your-retirement-back-on-track)
- Paying down high-interest debt
- [Honeymoon savings](https://www.northwest.bank/link/b5eb07812fca4f898a3aae540ca5a2c5.aspx?article_source=news_insights&amp%3Barticle_category=education&amp%3Barticle_name=how-to-plan-a-wedding-that-fits-your-budget&amp%3Barticle_cta=honeymoon-savings)
- [Down payment/home savings](https://financialwellnesscenter.northwest.bank/home-ownership/buying-a-home/article/going-from-renting-to-buying)
- Other large upcoming expenses


Create separate savings buckets or accounts for different goals, so wedding money doesn’t accidentally become emergency money or vice versa.


If family members make offers to contribute money, now is the time to have an upfront conversation about it. Does the money come with expectations or conditions? Do they expect repayment? Do they know how much they can offer?


When saving and spending for your wedding, it can be tempting to finance major purchases through credit cards or loans. Before borrowing, consider the interest, monthly payment and how long you’ll be repaying the balance after the wedding. A wedding is a celebration, but starting married life with expensive debt can make the celebration harder to enjoy in retrospect. A clear budget can help you spend on what matters without losing sight of the goals that will remain after the wedding.


## Build a wedding savings timeline


Once you know roughly how much you’ll spend on your wedding, work backward from the date to determine your timeline.


**Remaining amount needed / Months until the wedding = Monthly savings target**


For example, if you still need $15,000 and have 12 months before the wedding, your monthly savings goal would be $1,250.


*Use Northwest’s[savings goal calculator](https://financialwellnesscenter.northwest.bank/money-management/saving/tools/save-towards-a-goal?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=how-to-plan-a-wedding-that-fits-your-budget&article_cta=savings-goal-calculator) to estimate how much you may need to save each month.*


That’s your monthly savings goal. If that number doesn’t feel realistic, it’s information, not a failure.


As a couple, you have a few options:


- Extend the timeline and find a later date
- Reduce the guest list to lower the budget
- Revisit your priorities and find lower-cost alternatives


You might also reduce certain expenses, reconsider the date or try a short[no-spend challenge](https://financialwellnesscenter.northwest.bank/money-management/budgeting/article/what-is-the-no-buy-challenge) to put more toward your goal.


Remember, your budget and savings progress are living documents. They should change as your circumstances change.


## The wedding-day question to keep coming back to


When you find yourself fretting over expenses or stressed out over saving, ask yourself, “Years from now, what do you actually want to remember?”


It might be a fun night on the dance floor, a meal with the people you love or photographs you can look back on.


Your answer can help you distinguish between spending that supports your priorities and spending driven by trends or outside expectations. A meaningful wedding isn’t defined by the size of the budget. It reflects who you are as a couple and allows you to begin married life feeling more comfortable with what you spent.
